name: Sternocleidomastoid
func: The strap-like muscle running down each side of the neck. One side turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head; both together bend the neck forward.

levels.kid:
Turn your head to one side and look in a mirror. See the thick stripe that pops out on the side of your neck? That is the **sternocleidomastoid**. It is a really long name for a muscle!

It goes from the bone behind your **ear** down to your **collarbone** and the middle of your chest.

It helps you **turn your head** to look left and right, and **nod** your head forward. You have one on each side. It also helps you breathe in really hard when you have been running fast.
levels.hs:
The **sternocleidomastoid (SCM)** is a long muscle on each side of the neck, named after its three attachments: the **sternum**, the **clavicle** ("cleido") and the **mastoid process** of the skull.

It has two heads below. The **sternal head** is a rounded tendon from the top front of the **manubrium** of the sternum; the **clavicular head** is a broader, flat band from the inner third of the clavicle. A small gap between them sits over the internal jugular vein. The heads join and run up and back to insert on the **mastoid process** (the bump behind the ear) and the outer part of the **superior nuchal line**.

It lies just under the skin and the thin **platysma** muscle, with the **external jugular vein** crossing over it. It divides the neck into the **anterior triangle** in front and the **posterior triangle** behind. Underneath it run the **carotid artery**, **internal jugular vein** and **vagus nerve** inside the carotid sheath.

Acting on one side, it tilts the head toward the same shoulder and **rotates the face to the opposite side**. Acting together, both SCMs **flex the neck** and can lift the sternum during forced breathing. It is supplied by the **spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)**.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** sternal head from the anterior surface of the manubrium; clavicular head from the superior surface of the medial third of the clavicle. Insertion: the lateral surface of the mastoid process and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line.

**Actions in detail:** unilateral contraction produces ipsilateral lateral flexion and **contralateral rotation** of the head. Bilateral contraction flexes the lower cervical spine and brings the head forward, but because the insertion lies behind the axis of the atlanto-occipital joints, the SCMs can **extend** the head at the upper cervical joints when the neck is already extended. Its role is therefore position-dependent. With the head fixed, both muscles elevate the sternum and clavicles as **accessory muscles of inspiration**.

**Innervation:** motor from the **spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)**, which pierces or passes deep to the upper SCM before crossing the posterior triangle; proprioceptive fibres arrive from **C2–C3**. Blood supply is segmental: branches of the **occipital**, **superior thyroid** and **suprascapular** arteries.

**Landmarks:** the triangle between the two heads and the clavicle (the **lesser supraclavicular fossa**) overlies the internal jugular vein and is used for central line placement. The midpoint of the posterior border of SCM is **Erb's point**, where cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves) emerge. The carotid pulse is felt anterior to the SCM at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.
levels.phd:
The SCM's control by a cranial nerve whose motor neurons sit in the cervical cord is one of neuroanatomy's oddities. The SCM's motor neurons occupy the rostral part of the **spinal accessory nucleus** (roughly C1–C2/C3), while trapezius motor neurons extend more caudally, giving a rough rostrocaudal map.

Supranuclear control is debated. Clinical observations of hemispheric stroke and studies with **transcranial magnetic stimulation** suggest that each hemisphere drives the **ipsilateral SCM** more strongly (or bilaterally), in contrast to the predominantly contralateral control of trapezius. A proposed explanation is a double-crossing pathway in the brainstem. Functionally this makes sense: turning the head toward the left, a "leftward" action, requires the right SCM, which would be driven by the right hemisphere, the same hemisphere that moves the left limbs, keeping head and limb orientation linked.

The SCM is also a key effector in **cervical dystonia** (spasmodic torticollis), the most common focal dystonia. Abnormal basal ganglia–cerebellar network output produces sustained involuntary contraction of the SCM, splenius capitis and other neck muscles. Research using EMG mapping and neuroimaging targets which muscles drive each pattern (torticollis, laterocollis, anterocollis).

In infants, **congenital muscular torticollis** is associated with fibrosis of the SCM, sometimes as a firm mass (a "pseudotumour"). Proposed causes include intrauterine positioning, birth trauma and compartment-like ischaemia; histology shows fibroblast proliferation with muscle degeneration, and myoblast-like cells within the mass suggest a disturbed regenerative process.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** ask the patient to turn the head against your hand; the **opposite** SCM stands out, so turning left tests the right SCM. Test neck flexion against resistance for both SCMs. Inspect for wasting and asymmetry, and palpate the anterior triangle for nodes.

**Torticollis (wry neck):** the head tilts toward the affected side and the chin points to the opposite side. In infants with **congenital muscular torticollis**, a firm SCM mass may be felt; most improve with stretching and positioning, and persistent cases are released surgically. Always consider differentials such as cervical spine anomalies (**Klippel–Feil**), ocular torticollis (head tilt from a fourth nerve palsy) and, in children with sudden torticollis, infection such as **retropharyngeal abscess** or **atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation** (Grisel syndrome after throat infection). **Cervical dystonia** in adults is often treated with targeted botulinum toxin injections and physiotherapy.

**Nerve lesions:** a peripheral CN XI injury weakens the SCM and trapezius on the same side. In **myasthenia gravis** and some muscular dystrophies (notably **myotonic dystrophy**), SCM wasting gives a thin "swan neck".

**Surgical landmark:** the anterior border of the SCM is the line of incision for carotid endarterectomy and approaches to the anterior cervical spine. In **radical neck dissection**, the SCM, internal jugular vein and CN XI were classically removed; modified dissections preserve them where cancer allows.

In respiratory distress, prominent SCM use while breathing in signals increased work of breathing, a sign worth noting in asthma or COPD.

keyPoints: Runs from sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process
One side: tilts head to same side, turns face to opposite side
Both: flex the neck; accessory muscle of breathing
Divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles

test.q: Contracting the right sternocleidomastoid turns the face toward which side?
test.explain: Unilateral SCM rotates the face to the opposite side.

test.q: The bump behind the ear where the SCM inserts is the ______ process.
test.explain: The SCM is named for sternum, clavicle and mastoid.

test.q: Which nerve gives motor supply to the SCM?
test.explain: CN XI supplies both SCM and trapezius.

test.q: In congenital muscular torticollis, the infant's chin typically points:
test.explain: The head tilts toward the affected side and the chin rotates away.

test.q: The SCM divides the neck into the anterior and ______ triangles.
test.explain: The trapezius forms the back border of the posterior triangle.
